rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umar set out to kill Muhammad, but hearing his sister recite Sūrat Ṭā Hā changed him and he accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: خرج عمر بن الخطاب - رضي الله عنه - يريد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh sent ʿUtba to negotiate; after Muhammad recited verses from Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda, ʿUtba returned with a changed demeanor.
rows.anchor: أرسلوه بها , فقرأ عليه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم آيات من حم السجدة ,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the pilgrimage season, a group of Anṣār heard the Prophet recite, believed, and carried Islam back to Medina, where they made it public.
rows.anchor: ولما قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم القرآن في الموسم على النفر الذين حضروه من الأنصار آمنوا به وعادوا إلى المدينة فأظهروا الدين بها

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A report says the provinces were opened by swords, while Medina was opened by the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وقد روي عن بعضهم أنه قال: فتحت الأمصار بالسيوف وفتحت المدينة بالقرآن.

rows.speaker: الجن
rows.claim: The jinn heard the Qur’an and declared it wondrous, guiding to right direction, so they believed in it.
rows.anchor: ولما سمعته الجن لم تتمالك أن قالت: {إنا سمعنا قرآنا عجبا يهدي إلى الرشد فآمنا به}

words: تقشعر منه جلود الذين يخشون ربهم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s power to move receptive hearers is among its great signs and proofs of its miraculous character, as shown by several verses describing its effects.
rows.anchor: وهو من عظيم آياته , ودلائل معجزاته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elephant parody raises grand expectations but then dwells only on trunk and tail, omitting the creature’s intelligence, obedience, tusks, ears, and intricate design.
rows.anchor: وإذ قد دلك فيالة رأيك وسوء اختيارك على معارضة القرآن العظيم بذكر الفيل وأوصافه , فهلا أتيت منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Analogy is judged by shared meanings rather than physical size: elephant and mosquito share animal functions and head and trunk features, while the mosquito’s wings offset its small body.
rows.anchor: مدار الحكم في باب التشبيه والتمثيل على المعاني دون الأعيان والأجسام , والبعوض حيوان من أوجه كالفيل

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: The language authority al-Aṣmaʿī avoided explaining rare Qur’anic words; asked about “قد شغفها حباً,” he cited an Arab idiom but gave no fuller gloss.
rows.anchor: فكان الأصمعي - وهو إمام أهل اللغة - لا يفسر شيئا من غريب القرآن.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet urged people to learn Qur’anic inflection and seek out its unusual vocabulary; no grading is given.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " أعربوا القرآن والتمسوا غرائبه ".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh recognized the demands of the Qur’anic challenge and their inability to meet them, so they abandoned verbal contest and resorted to fighting.
rows.anchor: فتركوا المعارضة لعجزهم , وأقبلوا على المحاربة لجهلهم

rows.speaker: معترض
rows.claim: An objector argues that most Qur’anic language is ordinary Arabic and that eloquent Arabs could have matched it, but chose war to avoid a prolonged contest and dispute over merit.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل: إنا إذا تلونا القرآن وتأملناه وجدنا معظم كلامه مبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “a camel’s measure,” the verbal noun “measure” stands for a passive participle, as in “a dirham struck by the prince” or “cloth woven in Yemen.”
rows.anchor: والمصادر توضع موضع الأسماء كقولهم: هذا درهم ضرب الأمير وهذا ثوب نسج اليمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “An easy measure” means obtainable extra provisions if the brothers bring their younger brother, since each person was otherwise allotted only one camel-load during famine; “easy” means accessible, as poetic usage confirms.
rows.anchor: واليسير شائع الاستعمال فيما يسهل من الأمور كالعسير فيما يتعذر منها , ولذلك قيل يسر الرجل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes “easy measure” to mean quick service without delay, since Joseph gave the brothers priority while others waited.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل في ذلك: كيل يسير أي سريع لا حبس فيه , وذلك أن القوم كانوا يحبسون

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās reports that “measure” can mean price, as in the question “How is the measure with you?” meaning “How is the price?”; a line about Yāmāma and Miyāfāriqīn is cited.
rows.anchor: أخبرني أبو عمر عن أبي العباس قال: والكيل بمعنى السعر , كيف الكيل عندكم؟ أي: كيف السعر؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Walk on” suits the call to persist in their familiar practice calmly; “go forth” or “set out” would add agitation that conflicts with remaining steadfast and disregarding Muhammad.
rows.anchor: بل المشي في هذا المحل أولى وأشبه بالمعنى , وذلك لأنه إنما قصد به الاستمرار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further interpretation takes “walking” here as increasing in number and gathering to support their gods, rather than literal walking.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل المشي هاهنا معناه التوفر في العدد والاجتماع للنصرة دون المشي الذي هو نقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tests servants’ obedience and effort in collecting the Qur’an’s dispersed material and arranging it, thereby raising the ranks of believers and the learned.
rows.anchor: وقد أحب الله عز وجل أن يمتحن عباده ويبلو طاعتهم واجتهادهم في جمع المتفرق منه , وفي تنزيله وترتيبه

rows.speaker: معترض
rows.claim: The suggestion that an imitation was once made but later concealed is rejected: suppressing news of such a momentous event defies ordinary transmission, as would hiding other prophets and revealed laws.
rows.anchor: هذا سؤال ساقط. والأمر فيه خارج عما جرت به عادات الناس

rows.speaker: معترض
rows.claim: An objector offers alleged short imitations: Musaylima’s frog verse, an anonymous passage about a pregnant woman and infant, and a parody about the elephant.
rows.anchor: نحو ما حكي عن مسيلمة من قوله: " يا ضفدع نقي كم تنقين , لا الماء تكدرين ولا الوارد تنفرين "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musaylima’s frog passage has no sound wording or coherent meaning and meets none of eloquence’s three conditions; its forced rhyme subordinates sense to cadence.
rows.anchor: أما قول مسيلمة في الضفدع فمعلوم أنه خال من كل فائدة , لا لفظه صحيح , ولا معناه مستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an unattributed poetic exchange about wine, a reviser adds its value as sought-after wealth, pleasure, and relief from sorrow; the listener accepts the repair and vows to keep it.
rows.anchor: ولولا ثلاث هن في الكأس أصبحت ... كأنفس مال يستفاد ويطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Literary comparison can rank poets within a subject rather than require direct imitation: each may excel in a genre, and the stronger is the one who captures its details and fine meanings most fully.
rows.anchor: قلت: وها هنا وجه آخر يدخل في هذا الباب , وليس بمحض المعارضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once the conditions and forms of rhetorical contest are understood, it is clear that the Quraysh produced no genuine answer to the Qur’an’s challenge.
rows.anchor: قلت: وإذا أنت وقفت على شروط المعارضات ورسومها , وتبينت مذاهبها ووجوهها علمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elephant parody’s “What is the elephant?” opening promises an immense subject but ends with trunk and tail; unlike the Qur’anic openings on the Resurrection, it fails to fulfill its grand framing.
rows.anchor: أما علمت يا عاجز أن مثل هذه الفاتحة إنما تجعل مقدمة لأمر عظيم الشأن فائت الوصف متناهي الغاية في معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl’s distinction is valid when contrasted: “sit” follows reclining, whereas “sit down” follows standing; the paired terms are not interchangeable in every context.
rows.anchor: فقد حكى لنا النضر بن شميل أنه دخل على المأمون عند مقدمه من مرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Balā” answers a negatively framed question and affirms its denied proposition, as in the covenant; “naʿam” answers a question framed with “hal,” as in the question about God’s promise.
rows.anchor: فإن بلى جواب عن استفهام بحرف النفي كقول القائل: ألم تفعل كذا؟

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says “balā” only answers a question containing negation; had the primordial offspring answered “naʿam,” they would all have disbelieved.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: بلى لا يكون إلا جوابا عن مسألة يدخلها طرف من الجحد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative “dhāk” points to something near the speaker, whereas “dhālik” is used for something farther away.
rows.anchor: وأما قولك: ذاك وذلك فإن الإشارة بذلك إنما تقع إلى الشيء القريب منك , وذلك إنما يستعمل فيما كان متراخيا عنك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Min” and “ʿan” differ in common usage: taking money is from someone, taking knowledge is on their authority; hearing speech from someone is direct, while hearing a report about them is mediated, though the particles sometimes overlap.
rows.anchor: وأما من وعن فإنهما يفترقان في مواضع كقولك: أخذت منه مالا , وأخذت عنه علما

rows.speaker: أبو العالية؛ الحسن
rows.claim: Asked what heedlessness in prayer means, Abū al-ʿĀliya says losing track of whether one has prayed an even or odd number of units; al-Ḥasan rejects this and says it means letting the prayer time pass.
rows.anchor: قال رجل يا أبا العالية قول الله في كتابه: {فويل للمصلين الذين هم عن صلاتهم ساهون}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imitator wrongly uses “faʿala” for the favor of pregnancy, since the expression typically evokes punishment; wording such as “showed kindness” or “bestowed favor” fits the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: فإن أول ما غلط به هذا الجاهل أنه وضع كلمة الانتقام في موضع كلمة الإنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parody misapplies the verse about seminal fluid emerging between loins and ribs: the later child does not emerge from the ribs and entrails, but develops within the womb, which anatomy places between bladder and rectum.
rows.anchor: فإنما تعاطى استراقا من قول الله تعالى: {خلق من ماء دافق يخرج من بين الصلب والترائب}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an recounts successive stages in the womb, ending in a new created form with image and spirit; this displays God’s power, subtle wisdom, and abundant mercy.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر في آية أخرى عدد انتقالاته في الرحم من نطفة إلى علقة إلى مضغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A distinctive proof of the Qur’an’s inimitability is its effect on hearts: its sweetness and majesty can turn intended killers among the Arabs into allies and believers.
rows.anchor: قلت في إعجاز القرآن وجها آخر ذهب عنه الناس فلا يكاد يعرفه إلا الشاذ من آحادهم , وذلك صنيعه بالقلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan’s reading is preferred: “ʿan ṣalātihim” means neglecting the appointed time; confusion over units happens during prayer and would be expressed with “fī ṣalātihim.”
rows.anchor: فلو كان هو المراد لقيل: في صلاتهم ساهون , فلما قال عن صلاتهم دل على أن المراد به الذهاب عن الوقت

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutaybī wrongly derives “yaʿshu” from looking toward a fire; the phrase means turning away from the remembrance, not looking toward it, a distinction marked by “ʿan” versus “ilā.”
rows.anchor: زعم أنه من قوله: عشوت إلى النار أعشو إذا نظرت إليها. فغلطوه في ذلك

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, the Prophet distinguishes freeing one enslaved person outright from contributing toward the purchase price to emancipate someone.
rows.anchor: عن البراء بن عازب أن أعرابيا جاء

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī permits two forms equating the hornet and scorpion with “iyyā”; al-Ḥasan’s gathered Bedouin authorities reject his usage, siding with Sībawayh.
rows.anchor: فألقى سيبويه على الكسائي مسألة فقال: هل يجوز قول القائل: كاد الزنبور يكون العقرب

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh’s analysis is preferred because “iyyā” is used only in the accusative, while the disputed expression requires a nominative form; the Bedouin judges confirm his view.
rows.anchor: قيل وذلك أن حرف (إيا) إنما يستعمل في موضع النصب , وهي هنا في موضع رفع فلم يجز.

words: ولو أن قرآنا سيرت به الجبال أو قطعت به الأرض أو كلم به الموتى
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted answer in “If a Qur’an could move mountains…” is apt brevity: the context makes clear that this Qur’an would be that book, so the answer need not be spoken.
rows.anchor: وإنما جاز حذف الجواب في ذلك وحسن لأن المذكور منه يدل على المحذوف والمسكوت عنه من جوابه

words: ولو أن قرآنا سيرت به الجبال
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported view says leaving the answer unstated is even more eloquent because the listener’s imagination can range more widely than if one answer were specified.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إن الحذف في مثل هذا أبلغ من الذكر لأن النفس تذهب في الحذف كل مذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted answer at the gates of Paradise means that, once the God-fearing enter, they attain lasting bliss without interruption or disturbance.
rows.anchor: والمعنى كأنه قيل: لما دخلوها حصلوا على النعيم المقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition is blameworthy when it adds no meaning, but fitting when important matters need emphasis to prevent error, forgetfulness, or disregard; examples include repeated exhortations, labels, and a poetic line about Kinda.
rows.anchor: عجل عجل , وارم ارم , كما يكتب في الأمور المهمة على ظهور الكتب: مهم مهم مهم
